title: Strings
summary: A string stores text, and JavaScript provides tools to read and change that text.

subtopics.title: Text values
subtopics.explanation: A string is text and can use single quotes, double quotes, or backticks. For example, `"Hello"` and `'Hello'` both hold text. Choose a consistent quote style; use escapes when the text contains the same quote mark. Strings are immutable, so a method returns a new value rather than editing the original. Use a consistent quote convention so punctuation is easy to read. Escape a quote only when necessary, and avoid complex concatenation when a template literal is clearer. Quotation marks are like the edges of a note that show where its text begins and ends.

subtopics.title: Template literals
subtopics.explanation: A template literal uses backticks and can insert an expression with `${...}`. For example, `` `Hello, ${name}` `` includes the current value of `name`. This is convenient for messages, but a template string does not escape HTML. If the value is user-controlled, insert it as text or use a safe framework rendering path. Interpolation inserts a value into text but does not make that value safe HTML. A framework’s text rendering or a safe DOM API should handle user-controlled content. A template literal is like filling a blank in a greeting card with a name.

subtopics.title: Length
subtopics.explanation: `.length` reports the number of UTF-16 code units, which may differ from the number of visible characters. A common emoji can occupy more than one code unit. For ordinary checks, length is useful; for product limits based on what people perceive as a character, use Unicode-aware segmentation. JavaScript counts UTF-16 code units, so some visible emoji count as more than one. Match the counting method to the user-facing requirement. String length is like counting marks on a page, not always the characters a reader sees.

subtopics.title: Methods
subtopics.explanation: String methods such as `.toUpperCase()` return a changed string; they do not change the original. Save the result if the interface should display it. Language rules can affect capitalization and sorting, so use locale-aware APIs for names and text that depend on the user’s language. Formatting returns a new string. Store that result when it should be displayed, and use locale-sensitive APIs for language-specific casing or sorting. A string method is like making a marked-up copy while keeping the original note.

subtopics.title: Validation
subtopics.explanation: Check required text after considering spaces and user input. A string containing only spaces is still truthy. Trim it when leading and trailing spaces are not meaningful, but preserve them when the content requires them. This distinction matters for names, passwords, code, and other exact text. Validation rules should explain what counts as empty. Trimming is appropriate for many names, but passwords or code may need exact whitespace preserved. Checking trimmed text is like confirming a form is not blank just because it contains spaces.

foundations.overview: A string is a JavaScript value that represents text. Strings can contain names, messages, labels, or data from a form. Think of one as a line of written characters. You can combine or inspect strings, but they are immutable: methods return a new string rather than changing the original. Validate text before treating it as a required value.
foundations.whyItMatters: Text handling affects nearly every page. Clear validation and safe formatting prevent confusing messages and assumptions about how people type or read different languages.
foundations.browserPerspective: The engine stores strings as UTF-16 code units and often interns or shares identical string literals for efficiency. Because strings are immutable, the engine can safely reuse them, but building a long string by repeated concatenation can create many intermediate strings.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Formatting display text with template literals, validating emails with includes/indexOf, parsing CSV with split, sanitizing input with trim, and normalizing case with toLowerCase are constant tasks in UI and API code.
foundations.businessImpact: String bugs surface directly to users as broken messages, mis-parsed input, or failed validation, so reliable string handling protects the user experience and data quality.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Knowing the right method (slice vs substring, includes vs indexOf, replace vs replaceAll) prevents subtle off-by-one and 'only-replaced-the-first-match' bugs that are easy to miss.
foundations.performanceImpact: Because strings are immutable, heavy concatenation in loops allocates many temporary strings; collecting parts in an array and joining once, or using template literals, is friendlier to memory.
commonUseCases: Building display messages with template literals
Validating or searching input with includes/indexOf
Parsing text into parts with split
Normalizing input with trim and toLowerCase

commonMisconceptions.myth: String methods modify the original string.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Strings are immutable; methods like toUpperCase and replace return a new string, so you must reassign to keep the result.

commonMisconceptions.myth: replace swaps every occurrence of a substring.
commonMisconceptions.reality: replace with a plain string changes only the first match; use a global regex (/x/g) or replaceAll to change all occurrences.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A string method changes the original text in place.
commonMisconceptions.reality: JavaScript strings are immutable; methods return a new string value.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A non-empty string contains useful text.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Whitespace-only input is truthy, so trim or validate according to the user-facing requirement.

visualExplorer.title: How slicing a string produces a new string
visualExplorer.caption: See why string methods never change the original — they return a fresh copy.

config.intro: Follow `const upper = name.slice(0, 4)` on the string 'JavaScript'.

steps.name: Start with the original
steps.detail: name holds 'JavaScript', indexed J=0, a=1, v=2, a=3, S=4...

steps.name: Call slice(0, 4)
steps.detail: slice reads characters from index 0 up to (but not including) index 4.

steps.name: Build a new string
steps.detail: The engine creates a brand-new string 'Java' from those characters.

steps.name: Original is untouched
steps.detail: name still equals 'JavaScript' — slice did not modify it.

steps.name: Assign the result
steps.detail: The returned 'Java' is stored in the new variable; this is why you must capture the return value.

interactiveExamples.title: Template literals for clean messages
interactiveExamples.explanation: Embed variables and expressions directly with ${ } instead of stitching strings together with +.

interactiveExamples.title: Immutability in action
interactiveExamples.explanation: Methods return new strings; the original is never changed. You must reassign to keep the transformed value.

sandbox.code:
let title = 'hello world';
title.toUpperCase();          // result is ignored
console.log(title);           // still 'hello world'

title = title.toUpperCase();  // reassign
console.log(title);           // 'HELLO WORLD'

interactiveExamples.title: Searching and extracting
interactiveExamples.explanation: Combine indexOf, includes, and slice to find and pull out part of a string.

codeLab.title: Capitalize the first letter
codeLab.instructions: Write capitalize(str) that returns the string with its first character uppercased and the rest unchanged. Use slice and toUpperCase. Remember strings are immutable.
hints: Get the first character with str[0] and uppercase it.
Use str.slice(1) for the rest, then concatenate the two parts.

keyTakeaways: A string is text and can use single quotes, double quotes, or backticks.
A template literal uses backticks and can insert an expression with `${.
Check required text after considering spaces and user input.
